query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloy protective coatings achieve superior wear resistance because sliding wear conditions trigger the in-situ formation of a self-organized, nanostructured oxide (or glaze) layer that adapts to local stresses, thereby reducing adhesive and abrasive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited high-entropy alloy coating with a homogeneous solid-solution matrix and dispersed intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Modify the testing environment by comparing wear performance in ambient air (oxidizing conditions) versus an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) and/or adjust the alloy composition to alter oxidation kinetics.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed at room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures under consistent load and speed conditions that replicate practical wear situations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, nanostructured oxide or glaze layer on the coating surface during wear.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding wear, frictional heating and localized stresses accelerate the oxidation of selective elements based on their redox potentials and atomic sizes. This leads to the self-organization of an adaptive oxide layer that minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact and mitigates both adhesive and abrasive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings tested under oxidizing conditions (ambient air) will form a protective oxide layer, resulting in a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate compared to those tested in an inert atmosphere or coatings with compositions less prone to oxidation.
generation.baseline: Coatings with minimal in-situ oxide formation, either due to testing in inert atmospheres or alloy compositions that suppress oxidation, are expected to exhibit higher friction coefficients and wear rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for high-entropy alloy coatings designed with a balance of elements that allow selective oxidation. It may not be effective if the operating temperature is so high that the oxide layer becomes mechanically unstable or if the alloy composition completely resists oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise composition and microstructural characteristics of the optimal oxide layer are not fully determined, and the quantitative thresholds for effective wear resistance remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct controlled sliding wear tests on the high-entropy alloy coating under two conditions: (a) in ambient air to allow oxidation and (b) in an inert argon atmosphere. Additionally, test coatings with modified compositions that are less prone to oxidation. Compare friction coefficients, wear rates, and surface microstructures post-test.
measurements: Surface characterization (SEM, XRD, TEM) to assess the presence and continuity of the oxide/glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxide layer fails to form in ambient air or if there is no significant difference in wear performance between oxidizing and inert atmospheres (or between coatings with and without elements promoting oxidation), then the hypothesis—that adaptive oxide layer formation governs wear resistance—is falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys

Abstract: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. Frictional Wear and Corrosion Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Synthesized by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloy coatings (HEAC) exhibit good frictional wear and corrosion resistances, which are of importance for structure materials. In this study, the microstructure, surface morphology, hardness, frictional wear and corrosion resistance of an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coating synthesized by atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) were investigated. The frictional wear and corrosion resistance of the coating are simultaneously improved with an increase of the power of APS. The influence of the APS process on the microstructure and mechanical behavior is elucidated. The mechanisms of frictional wear and corrosion behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi HEAC are discussed in detail.Keywords: high-entropy alloy, coatings, atmospheric plasma spraying, frictional wear, corrosion
